header_title: The Jiggle That Holds You Up
question_text: If an atom is mostly empty space why does a solid feel solid?
audio_script: Look at your hand. Solid. But inside it is mostly empty space - atoms as far apart as trees in a forest. Yet the hand feels solid. Why? The atoms jiggle. They are always moving, always bumping. Squeeze them and they push back, not because they are hard like marbles, but because that jiggling has energy and the energy has to go somewhere. The same thing keeps you from falling through the floor. Your chair resists you because its atoms refuse to stop moving. It is not the atoms themselves that are hard. It is their motion. You are sitting on a cloud of quantum jitter, and it holds you up.

header_title: What Is a Magnet Really?
question_text: Where does a magnet's pull actually come from?
audio_script: Hold a magnet near a compass. The needle swings. But there is no magic. Inside that iron a billion billion electrons spin, all pointing the same way. Each one is a tiny current loop. Add them all up and you get the magnet's field. That field reaches out through empty space and turns the compass needle so its own electrons line up too. Nothing touches anything. The pull travels through nothing. Imagine a city of tiny spinning dancers, all turning the same way, and their collective motion reaches across the table to nudge another dancer's feet. Your fridge magnet is doing this right now.

header_title: Why Atoms Don't Collapse
tagline: The wobble that keeps you alive
question_text: If opposites attract why doesn't the electron fall into the proton?
audio_script: In a hydrogen atom one electron circles one proton. Opposite charges. Common sense says the electron should fall straight in. In a fraction of a second the atom should collapse. But it does not. Why? Quantum mechanics. If the electron sits still it has to be somewhere tiny, and a tiny position means huge uncertainty in its speed. Huge speed means enormous energy. So the electron pays to stay far away, where the uncertainty is smaller. Electric pull wants to draw it close. Quantum jitter keeps pushing it back. Balance. Remove the jitter and every atom in the universe vanishes in a flash.

header_title: The Invisible Web
question_text: What actually exists in the empty space between two magnets?
audio_script: What is the space between two magnets? Empty, right? Yet something crosses it. Faraday imagined an invisible web. At every point in space, an arrow. The arrow says: if a charge arrives here, push it this way. That is a field. Not a substance. Not a wind. A rule. Every point in the universe has a rule. Your phone's signal is a rule. The light of a star is a rule. The tug of a magnet is a rule. Maxwell's equations tell the rules how to change. That is the whole story. A field is not a thing that fills space. It is a way space is organised.

header_title: What Is Light Made Of?
question_text: How does light cross a vacuum with nothing to travel through?
audio_script: Light is not a stream of bullets. It is a wave, but a wave of what? Not water. Not air. Of fields. An electric field wiggling, a magnetic field wiggling, in step. Wiggle the electric field and it creates a magnetic field. Wiggle the magnetic field and it creates an electric field. They feed each other forever, rushing through space at the speed of light. That is why starlight can cross billions of years of nothing and still land in your eye. Two wiggling arrows holding hands, running free. No medium, no ether, no invisible jelly. Just two fields in a dance.

header_title: The Curve Between Two Charges
tagline: How opposite charges reach each other
question_text: Why do water molecules grab onto their neighbours?
audio_script: Two charges. One positive one negative. They pull toward each other. But how do they know? The positive charge makes a field. The negative charge makes a field. Where the two fields overlap, they add. The total push, at every point in space, is toward the other charge. Snapshot the arrows and you see a pattern called a dipole: two centres, one family of lines curving between them. That curve is why a water molecule grabs its neighbours. It is why microwaves heat your dinner. It is why DNA holds its shape. Two little charges, one big consequence.

header_title: Why Wires Make Magnetism
question_text: Why does a current-carrying wire push a compass needle?
audio_script: In 1820 Oersted was lecturing on electricity. By accident his battery wire was near a compass. The needle jumped. He had discovered electromagnetism. Why does a wire move a magnet? Because current is moving charge, and a moving charge makes a magnetic field. Around the wire, the field makes circles. Those circles reach out and turn the compass needle so its own electrons line up. Nothing special about copper. Nothing special about iron. Any moving charge makes magnetism. Your phone's antenna, the coil of a motor, the glow of the aurora above the pole - all currents, all fields, one phenomenon.

header_title: Three Forces in a Knife-Edge Balance
question_text: If protons repel each other how can a nucleus hold together?
audio_script: Two protons in a nucleus are trying to fly apart. Their electric repulsion is billions of billions of billions of times stronger than gravity. But gravity is not what holds them. A third force, the strong force, is even stronger, but it only reaches across a tiny distance. Three forces in balance. Push one proton in and it repels. Push it hard enough and the strong force catches. If the balance were off by a hair, nothing we know would exist. Stars, tables, rocks - everything you have ever seen - hangs on this knife-edge.

header_title: Why Swings Slow Down
tagline: A rotation seen from the side
question_text: What is really happening when a pendulum swings back and forth?
audio_script: A swing at the park. Back and forth. Sometimes fast, sometimes slow, sometimes still. Its motion looks complicated. But there is a secret. Spin a wheel and watch one point on its rim from the side. That point looks like it is going back and forth. A swing is a rotation seen from the side. A simple oscillation is a spinning arrow projected onto a line. That is why we can describe a radio antenna with a rotating arrow called a phasor. Oscillations are rotations. Spin a wheel, watch a line, and you have a wave.

header_title: What a Force Actually Is
question_text: Two billiard balls, one rolling. What passes between them when they touch?
audio_script: Two billiard balls on a table. One is rolling. One sits still. They touch. Now both move. What passed between them? What changed was momentum - a push handed from one ball to the other. Newton called this a force. Something that changes motion. For two electrons the force is electric. For two planets it is gravity. For two magnets it is magnetism. Different rules. Same idea. Something changes the speed or direction of something else. Watch the balls. See the handoff. That handoff is a force. Force is always a verb. Always acting, always transferring.

header_title: How Strong Is a Balloon's Grip?
question_text: A rubbed balloon carries 1.6e-7 C. It is 3 mm from a wall whose surface charge is similar. What is the attractive force?
audio_script: You have seen this a hundred times. Rub a balloon on your hair. It gets charged. Touch it to a wall. It sticks. Hours. Why? Rubbing scrapes electrons off your hair. They hop onto the balloon. Now the balloon has extra negative charge. Maybe a trillion electrons. About 1.6 times ten to the minus seven coulombs. The wall is neutral. But its charges are not frozen. When the negative balloon approaches, the wall's electrons flee inward. The wall surface becomes slightly positive. Opposite charges attract. Now the number. Coulomb: k is nine times ten to the ninth. Each q is 1.6 times ten to the minus seven. r squared is nine times ten to the minus six. The product is about 2.6 times ten to the minus two newtons. Roughly the weight of a paper clip. Enough to hold the balloon.

header_title: How Big Is an Electron's Circle?
tagline: The secret inside an old TV
question_text: An electron with speed 3e7 m/s enters a 1 mT magnetic field at right angles. What is the radius of its circular path?
audio_script: You are watching an old TV. A beam of electrons sweeps across the screen. Magnets steer it. Why magnets? Because a magnetic field pushes on any moving charge. Not along its path. Sideways, perpendicular to velocity and to field. So the electron curves. Not a parabola, not a line. A circle. Why a circle? The magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, and a perpendicular force produces a circular path. So q v B equals m v squared over r. Cancel one v. r equals m v over q B. Every number is known. Mass: nine point one times ten to the minus thirty-one. Velocity: three times ten to the seventh. Charge: 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen. Field: one millitesla. Numerator about 2.7 times ten to the minus twenty-three. Denominator 1.6 times ten to the minus twenty-two. Divide: 0.17 metres. Seventeen centimetres. Big enough to see. That is why old TVs were deep.

header_title: What Is the Wavelength of Green Light?
question_text: Green light has frequency 6e14 Hz. What is its wavelength?
audio_script: You see green. Your eye reports a color. But the color is really a number. A frequency. About six hundred trillion oscillations per second. Six times ten to the fourteen. Every photon of that green light is a tiny wave, wiggling its electric and magnetic fields six hundred trillion times each second. How far does the wave travel in the time it takes to wiggle once? That is its wavelength. Light travels three times ten to the eighth metres per second. Frequency is six times ten to the fourteen. Divide. Three times ten to the eighth over six times ten to the fourteen. Five times ten to the minus seven metres. 500 nanometres. Half a micrometre. A thousandth of a hair. That is the wavelength of green light. Red is longer. Blue is shorter. Your eye is a wavelength detector.

header_title: Which Way Does the Needle Point?
question_text: Earth's field is 50 uT north. A wire 5 cm away produces 20 uT east. What is the direction of the combined field?
audio_script: A compass needle points north. Bring a wire with a current near it. The needle swings. Not all the way. Just partway. Why? The needle points along the total magnetic field. Now it is the sum of two fields. Earth's field points north at fifty microteslas. The wire's field points east at twenty microteslas. Add them as arrows. The needle follows the sum. The angle is the arctangent of twenty over fifty. Arctangent of zero point four. About twenty-two degrees east of north. Every current-carrying wire adds its own field. That is how a compass tells you a wire is live.

header_title: Flux Through a Surface That Misses the Charge
question_text: A +q charge sits just outside a closed spherical surface. What is the net electric flux through the surface?
audio_script: Gauss's law says flux through any closed surface equals enclosed charge over epsilon zero. A charge outside the surface? Zero. Why? Every field line that enters must exit. They are not created or destroyed in empty space. Pick a line skimming in. Follow it. It comes out. Count plus one. Count minus one. Zero. Put the charge inside. Every line starts on it and ends outside. The count of outbound lines equals charge over epsilon zero. The surface shape does not matter. Only what is inside.

header_title: Circulation of B Around a Wire
question_text: A long straight wire carries 2 A. A circular loop of radius 0.5 m circles it. What is the line integral of B around the loop?
audio_script: Ampere's law does not ask you to compute B. It asks for the integral. Mu zero is four pi times ten to the minus seven. Multiply by the enclosed current of two amperes. Eight pi times ten to the minus seven. Roughly 2.5 times ten to the minus six tesla metres. The radius does not appear. Any loop surrounding the wire gives the same integral. One metre, one kilometre, tangled, circular. Only when the wire is outside does the answer drop to zero. Ampere's law is a bookkeeping shortcut.

header_title: Which Way Does the Force Point?
question_text: An electron moves east through a magnetic field pointing north. Which direction is the magnetic force?
audio_script: Right-hand rule first. Index finger east. Middle finger north. Thumb points up. That would be the force on a positive charge. But our particle is an electron. Negative. Flip the direction. Down. This is the trap exams love. The rule is for a positive charge. For an electron the force is opposite. So the electron is pushed downward. This is why electrons in a cathode ray tube bend one way while protons bend the other for the same v and B.

header_title: Two Parallel Wires
question_text: Two long parallel wires, 2 A and 4 A in the same direction, 0.1 m apart. What is the force per unit length?
audio_script: Same-direction currents attract. Opposite-direction currents repel. That is the magnetic handshake. Now the magnitude. Mu zero times I one times I two over two pi d. Mu zero is four pi times ten to the minus seven. I one times I two is eight. Two pi d is two pi times zero point one. Cancel pi. Four times ten to the minus seven, times eight, over zero point two. That is 1.6 times ten to the minus five newtons per metre. Small but real. This is how current balances calibrate the ampere.

header_title: Rate of Change of E Between Capacitor Plates
question_text: A parallel-plate capacitor of area 0.01 m2 is charged at 5 A. What is dE/dt between the plates?
audio_script: Maxwell's displacement current equals epsilon zero times dE/dt times area. That must equal the actual current in the wire. Five amperes. So dE/dt equals I over epsilon zero times area. Five over eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve, times zero point zero one. Roughly five point six five times ten to the thirteen volts per metre per second. Staggering. But required. The changing E between the plates acts like a real current. That is why electromagnetic waves travel in vacuum. E changes create B. B changes create E. No charges needed.

header_title: Why Magnetism Is a Tiny Correction
tagline: The v2/c2 in the fine print
question_text: In a copper wire with electron drift speed 0.1 mm per second, what is v squared over c squared?
audio_script: Drift velocity is a tenth of a millimetre per second. Ten to the minus four metres per second. Square it. Ten to the minus eight. c squared is nine times ten to the sixteen. Divide. About ten to the minus twenty-five. Absurdly small. So why does magnetism matter? Because the electric field between moving electrons in two parallel wires is enormous. But it almost perfectly cancels the proton field. The cancellation is good to far better than ten to the minus twenty-five. Only the tiny leftover remains. That leftover is magnetism.
